Know Your Machine

How a CPU really works

Apple M5 Max · 6 performance + 12 efficiency cores · 128 GB unified · measured from scratch

A short course in what makes a processor fast or slow — taught entirely by measuring one. No spec sheets, no system call that hands you the answer. Just timed loops, and a few honest tricks.

The one rule: separate what you measure from what you assume. The only things truly measured are elapsed time and instruction counts. "GHz" and "cycles" are those divided, resting on one stated assumption — and the text always says so.

Chapter 1What is a clock cycle, and how fast does it tick?

A CPU is driven by a clock; one cycle is one tick. "4.5 GHz" means 4.5 billion ticks a second. On Apple Silicon you can't just read that number — the OS won't tell you, and the real hardware cycle counter is privileged. So we infer it, with the trick the whole course is built on:

Build a chain of dependent integer adds — each needs the previous one's result. The CPU can't start the next until this one finishes, and an add finishes in one cycle. So the chain runs at exactly one add per cycle, and adds-per-second = cycles-per-second = clock speed.
clock = ~4.57 GHz  — and a second, independent clock (the ARM system timer)
agrees with the OS timer to 0.00%, so the time is trustworthy.

What's measured vs assumed: we measured time and counted adds — solid. The leap to "GHz" assumes one dependent add equals one cycle. We can't prove that from userspace, but it lands exactly on the known P-core clock, so it's corroborated. The honest label is "billions of dependent adds per second," which we call GHz.

Chapter 2A single core does many things at once

Here's the fact that surprises almost everyone: the model of "fetch an instruction, do it, fetch the next" has been wrong for thirty years. A modern core is superscalar — several execution units firing in parallel. Take the dependent chain (1/cycle) and compare it to chains that don't depend on each other. Same 8 billion adds, one core:

adds per cycle, one core

1 dependent chain
1.0
8 independent
5.8

Same core, same adds, ~5× faster when they're independent — because the core ran several at once. The dependent chain wasn't slow because adds are slow; it was slow because each add had to wait. This is the course's first recurring theme: independence is speed.

Chapter 3…but only if it can see the parallelism

So why not more? A core finds independent work by looking ahead in the instruction stream, but only within a finite window. If each chain is emitted as one contiguous block, the independent work sits far away and the units go idle. Interleave the chains — put independent adds next to each other — and:

same 8 chains, two layouts · adds/cycle

blocked
3.3
interleaved
5.8

Identical work, merely reordered, and throughput jumps ~75% to the core's true width. This is exactly why compilers do instruction scheduling — and we just watched it earn its keep by hand.

Chapter 4Now multiply by all the cores

Chapters 2–3 lived inside one core. This chip has 18. Running the wide loop across 1→32 threads:

integer throughput (G/s) vs threads

It scales near-linearly to ~16 threads, then a dead-flat wall: 24 and 32 threads return the exact same 318 G/s, because there's no 19th core. That flat line is the hardware making its own count visible. Peak ≈ 318 billion adds/sec — 15× one core (not 18×: E-cores are slower and the chip shares one power budget).

Chapter 5The memory wall

Every add so far touched only registers. Real code reaches into memory, and that's where cores go to wait. A pointer chase — each load's address depends on the last, so nothing overlaps — exposes raw latency as the working set grows:

pointer-chase latency vs working set · cycles

The latency climbs in cliffs as the set outgrows each cache — the memory hierarchy, drawn by a stopwatch. An L1 hit costs 4 cycles; a DRAM miss ~425, over 100× worse. During one DRAM stall a 6-wide core could have run ~2,500 instructions; instead it's frozen, waiting for one number. This is why real code rarely nears the 318 G/s ceiling.

Chapter 6Access pattern beats working-set size

That was the worst case: random and dependent. Keep the buffer huge but make the accesses predictable — walk it in order instead of shuffled — and over the same 256 MB:

256 MB, two ways · ns per access

sequential
 
0.9 ns
random
96 ns
96 ns

Sequential is a flat line — a 256 MB walk costs the same as a 16 KB one, because the hardware prefetcher sees the stride and pulls each line in before you ask. Random is 109× slower. Size stopped mattering the instant access became predictable. (And independent streaming loads hit ~100 GB/s on one core — the Chapter 2 lesson again, on loads.)

Chapter 7Branches, and how a CPU "predicts" the future

A third way to stall: control flow. At an if, the pipelined core doesn't yet know which way to go — so it guesses, runs ahead, and pays ~15 cycles only if wrong. Summing the elements ≥128 of an array, sorted vs random — identical work, identical memory, only the data order differs:

cycles per element

sorted
1.5
alternating
1.5
random
4.7
branchless
1.0

The predictor isn't AI — it's a tiny circuit betting "do what this branch did last time," right ~95–99% of the time on real code. Sorted data makes the branch trivially predictable; random is a coin flip it can't beat, ~3× slower. It even nails alternating (proving it keys on the recent pattern, not luck) — only true randomness defeats it. Replace the branch with arithmetic (branchless) and the cost vanishes entirely.

Chapter 8SIMD: one instruction, many numbers

Every add so far handled one number. A 128-bit SIMD register holds four, and one instruction adds all four at once; with several SIMD units, the lanes multiply. One core:

integer adds per cycle, one core

scalar
5.9
NEON (4-wide)
16.6

A 2.8× jump on top of everything else, and 140 GFLOP/s of floating-point from a single core (all 4 FP units saturated). CPU SIMD is narrow — 4 to 16 lanes — so you loop over big data in small gulps. The "thousands at once" machine is the GPU (Chapter 12).

Chapter 9The hidden cache: address translation (TLB)

Every access uses a virtual address the hardware must translate to a physical one — and that translation is itself cached, in the TLB. Miss it and the core "walks the page tables," extra memory reads, even when the data is in L1. Chase the same number of cache lines packed vs spread one-per-page:

same 128 KB, in L1 both times · cycles/access

packed
 
3.8
spread
131
131

30× slower to read the same in-cache data — the data was never the problem; translating its address overflowed the TLB. Two caches work on every access: one for data, one hidden one for addresses, and you can blow either. (This is also why Apple's 16 KB pages buy a 4× bigger L1.)

Chapter 10All the way down: the SSD

Below DRAM is storage. A random SSD read takes 71 µs ≈ 315,000 cycles — ~760× slower than DRAM, ~80,000× slower than L1. But the headline is how you talk to it: every read is a system call with fixed overhead, so block size dominates.

reading the same 512 MB, by block size · GB/s

~100× faster from block size alone — reading in 4 MB gulps pays the syscall 128 times instead of 131,072. Same shape as every chapter: a fixed cost only hurts when you fail to batch or overlap around it.

Chapter 11The whole chip, for real

Measured across all 18 cores, the two ceilings behave completely differently. Compute scales to all 18 cores (1.9 TFLOP/s). Memory bandwidth does not:

streaming bandwidth (GB/s) vs threads

One core already pulls 104 GB/s — a third of the whole bus — and ~6 cores saturate it at ~300 GB/s; more cores buy nothing. This is the most practical lesson here: compute-bound work scales to all 18 cores; memory-bound work saturates at ~6 and flatlines. Throwing cores at a bandwidth-bound program is throwing them away.

Chapter 12The other processor: the GPU

The "thousands at once" machine. A 40-core GPU, ~5,000 lanes. It hits 14.9 TFLOP/s (~8× the CPU) and 578 GB/s — but watch what it takes to get there:

GPU FP32 throughput (TFLOP/s) vs threads launched

At 1,024 threads it manages 1.2 TFLOP/s — slower than the CPU; it doesn't wake up until ~250,000 threads are in flight. That's the whole CPU-vs-GPU distinction: a CPU hides latency with cleverness (out-of-order, prediction, prefetch — fast even single-threaded); a GPU hides it with sheer numbers (thousands of threads, so one is always runnable). Two opposite bets on the same problem — which is why your machine has both.

In one pictureThe whole machine

We started with the naive model — fetch one instruction, do it, fetch the next — and measured every layer stacked on top of it. The full ladder, top to bottom, every rung measured here:

the memory ladder · if one cycle were one second

tierlatencycycles= 1 cyc/sec
registers~0.2 ns~11 second
L10.9 ns44 seconds
L2~4 ns~2020 seconds
DRAM95 ns4257 minutes
SSD (random)71 µs~315,0003.6 days

It comes down to two knobs, both measured here. Independence — is there other work to overlap while you wait? A dependency chain pins you to 1×; independent work buys ~6–20×. Locality — is the data reachable cheaply? Up to ~100× between L1 and a random DRAM miss. Multiply them and you span ~2,000× from best-case compute to a random DRAM miss, ~300,000× down to the SSD. Which end your program lands on is decided mostly by data layout and access order, not how many instructions you write — and every mechanism in the chip exists to claw back one of those gaps.

Measured on this machine with timed loops — no spec sheets. "GHz" and "cycles" rest on one assumption (1 dependent add = 1 cycle), corroborated by landing on the known clock. Several figures are best-of-N (the hardware's ceiling); real workloads run further from every one. · know-your-machine
